entries.name: Pamphilus of Caesarea
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds Book I of his Apology for Origen, in the Latin of Rufinus. It has two printings, Lommatzsch of 1846 and Migne of 1857. Only that one book survives. Both scans are rough OCR, so every quote needs checking against the page.

Who wrote the Apology is disputed. Eusebius says he and Pamphilus wrote it together. Jerome, in his book against Rufinus, cites Eusebius as saying Pamphilus wrote nothing but some short letters. Years before, Jerome had listed it under Pamphilus's name. The Library counts a jointly written work as the person's own words. So it counts this one.

Fragments on the Acts of the Apostles are also ascribed to him. Others give them to Euthalius, so they are not counted. His dates are the years of his prison term and death. The Library's sources give no birth year.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Alexandrian teachers. He is said to have studied at Alexandria. He lived and died at Caesarea. There he kept Origen's books. The Library shelves his Apology with them.
entries.why: Pamphilus was a presbyter at Caesarea in Palestine. He gathered a library of sacred books and copied Origen's works by hand. He was jailed in 307 and put to death for his faith in 309 or 310. Eusebius, the church historian, took the surname Pamphili from their friendship.
entries.teaser: Caesarea in Palestine, c. 307 to 310 CE: a presbyter and book collector, put to death for his faith, whose defence of Origen Eusebius calls joint work and Jerome denies him.
entries.longDescription:
By the common account, Pamphilus studied at Alexandria under Pierius, the head of the catechetical school. Later he became a presbyter at Caesarea. Eusebius says he gave his goods to the needy and excelled all in his time in devotion to the Scriptures. Jerome says he copied most of Origen's works with his own hand. He also built a library of sacred books and gave it to the church at Caesarea.

In the persecution under Diocletian, the governor Urbanus jailed him near the end of 307. Eusebius says he and his friends lay in prison two full years. Then Firmilianus, the next governor, had him put to death. The usual date is 309. The English editor of Eusebius argues for February 310.

Rufinus put the first book of an Apology for Origen into Latin. He gave it Pamphilus's name alone. Eusebius says the two wrote it together. Jerome later said Eusebius wrote it all. He said Eusebius himself had written that Pamphilus wrote only letters. Yet he had once listed it as Pamphilus's. Editors of both say Pamphilus shared in it.
voices: Pamphilus — presbyter and martyr, whose Apology for Origen the Library holds in the Latin of Rufinus
Eusebius of Caesarea — his friend, who says the two wrote the Apology together
Jerome — who kept twenty-five volumes in Pamphilus's hand, and later denied that Pamphilus wrote the Apology
Rufinus — who put Book I into Latin and gave it under Pamphilus's name
entries.legacy:
Two later worlds in the Library name him. Eusebius, writing in the church of the Constantinian empire, calls him "the great glory of the parish of Cæsarea." Eusebius was his friend, so this voice stands close to Pamphilus's own circle.

Jerome, in his ascetic and literary circle, calls him a copyist.

He calls him the founder of the library at Caesarea. He says he found six volumes of Eusebius's Apology there.

He wrote against Rufinus that Eusebius himself says "Pamphilus wrote nothing except some short letters to his friends."

entries.name: Bonaventure
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds his Life of Saint Francis, the Legenda maior, in Salter's English of 1904. It also holds three Latin works from the Quaracchi edition of 1911. They are the Breviloquium, the Itinerarium mentis in Deum and the De reductione artium ad theologiam. The Latin scan has OCR slips, so check any quote against the page.

His dates are the years he led the Franciscans. They come from Glassberger's chronicle, an Observant work in Latin. The Library holds no source for his birth year. Glassberger's two chronicles disagree on the year he became a cardinal; the editors give 1273.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Franciscan movement. He did not found it. His own Life of Francis gives the founding of the Religion to Francis. He led the order as minister general, and the Life he wrote was meant to be its standard account of Francis.
entries.why: Bonaventure was a friar and a master of theology. He was elected minister general of the Franciscans in 1257 and led them until his death in 1274. He wrote the Life of Francis that the order meant to be its standard Life.
entries.teaser: Paris and Lyon, 1257 to 1274 CE: the Franciscan leader who wrote the life of Francis that the order meant to be its standard.
entries.longDescription:
Glassberger writes that the chapter at Rome elected Bonaventure minister general while he was away. He gives the year as 1256. The Quaracchi editors say that is the old count, and that by ours it was 1257. In 1273 Pope Gregory X named him a cardinal and bishop of Albano. The editors say he then went with the pope to Lyon for the council. Glassberger says he fell ill during the council and died there. The friars buried him in their church at Lyon.

In the prologue to his Life of Francis, Bonaventure says the urging of the Chapter General moved him to write it. He says that as a child he was snatched from death by calling on Francis, and by Francis's merits. To learn the true story, he went to the place of Francis's birth and talked with friends of his who were still alive. Salter's note says he wrote it between 1260 and 1263, and meant it to replace earlier Lives. She adds that another general chapter ordered the earlier Lives suppressed.

He did not found the movement. The third chapter of his Life treats the founding of Francis's Religion. In the prologue to the Itinerarium, he writes that he withdrew to Mount Alverna, near the day of Francis's death, to seek peace of spirit in a quiet place. There Francis had seen the vision of the seraph. The Quaracchi editors date that visit to 1259.
voices: Bonaventure — friar, master of theology and minister general, whose Life of Francis and three Latin works the Library holds
Francis of Assisi — the founder, whose life Bonaventure wrote at the Chapter General's urging
Nicolaus Glassberger — the Observant chronicler who records Bonaventure's chapters and orders
entries.legacy:
Later Catholic writers name him. Liguori, in The Glories of Mary, writes that "St. Bonaventure declares" that those who publish Mary's glories are sure of paradise. The sentence names no work of his.

Glassberger, a friar, tells of his chapters. In 1269, he says, Bonaventure held a general chapter at Assisi. It ordered that, out of reverence for the Virgin, a Mass be sung solemnly each Saturday, where this could fittingly be done.

English editors of the mystics name him too. In 1924 Justin McCann called him "a disciple of Richard" in his mystical teaching. This is Richard of St Victor. In 1914 Evelyn Underhill named him among three masters of Rolle. In 1923 she said Hilton depends on Bernard and Bonaventura, too.

entries.name: Heraclius
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing:
Moderate. The Library holds the Ecthesis, a statement of faith issued in his name. It stands in the Latin acts of the Lateran Council of 649, in Mansi's tenth volume. The scan is rough OCR, with a garbled Greek text beside the Latin. The Library counts a document issued in his name as his own words.

Who wrote the Ecthesis is disputed. The Lateran fathers say Sergius, the patriarch, persuaded Heraclius, then emperor, to put his name to it. A letter quoted in the volume's notes has Heraclius say it was not his own, that Sergius composed it, and that he agreed to set it out in his name with his signature. Two notes in Mansi place a synod of 638 as confirming it. His dates are the years of his reign. They come from two notes in the Library's texts.
entries.relationsSummary: Told within the Byzantine imperial church of the Heraclian and iconoclast eras. He was emperor from 610 to 641, as this church's age began. The Ecthesis was issued in his name. Sergius's synod confirmed it in 638. A council in 649 condemned it.
entries.why: Heraclius was emperor from 610 to 641. The Armenian bishop Sebeos says he took the Cross back to Jerusalem. In 638 a synod under Sergius confirmed a statement of faith issued in his name, the Ecthesis. It forbids anyone to speak of or teach one or two operations in Christ. It also calls the confession of two wills at odds in him impious. A Roman council condemned it in 649.
entries.teaser: Constantinople, 610 to 641 CE: the emperor who brought the Cross home. A statement of faith issued in his name was condemned by Rome.
entries.longDescription:
Macler's note to Sebeos says the patriarch Sergius crowned Heraclius on 6 October 610. A note in Mansi says he died on 11 February 641. Sebeos writes that the king received the holy Cross and brought it to Jerusalem, with all the church vessels that had escaped the enemy in Byzantium. There he set it back in its place, and put the church's objects back where they belonged. He says it stayed in the holy city until the sons of Ishmael took Jerusalem the second time.

The Ecthesis opens as a statement of faith made by Heraclius, because a dispute had arisen over the question of operation. It says it agrees with the five holy councils. It forbids anyone to speak of or teach one operation or two. It also calls it impious to confess two wills in Christ that come against each other.

The Lateran fathers of 649 say the Ecthesis was written in the name of Heraclius, then emperor, by enemies of the faith. They say Sergius persuaded Heraclius, then emperor, to put his name to it. A letter quoted in the Mansi notes has Heraclius say the Ecthesis is not his. He says he did not dictate it or order it made. Sergius wrote it five years earlier, before Heraclius came back from the East. When the emperor reached the city, Sergius asked him to set it out in his name, with his signature, and he agreed. The Lateran council anathematized the Ecthesis.
voices: Heraclius — emperor, in whose name the Ecthesis was issued; the Library holds it in the Lateran acts
Sergius — the patriarch who, the sources say, urged the Ecthesis on him
Sebeos — the Armenian bishop whose history tells of Heraclius and the Cross
Martin I — the pope whose Lateran council of 649 condemned the Ecthesis
entries.legacy:
Armenian writers name him. Giovanni de Serpos, in his history of 1786, says the Armenian patriarch Yezr held the council at Karin to please the emperor Heraclius and the Greek curopalates. He also gives the clergy's answer. They say the Armenians gave way from a wish for peace, from respect for Heraclius, from joy at his victories, and from a wish to win him as their defender against the Persians.

The Church of the East names him too. The Chronicle of Seert tells how Heraclius, whom it calls son of the master of Egypt, sailed to Constantinople, and how Phocas fell. It also records his death. The editor, Addai Scher, notes that the printed year should read 952 of Alexander. These writers name Heraclius for his war and his church policy.

wants: English rendering of Pamphilus's Apology for Origen, Book I (Rufinus's Latin): the Library has only the Latin, so the entry quotes no word of the Apology itself and cannot show his own voice in English.

A clean Latin edition of the Ecthesis, or a Greek text, in place of the OCR in Mansi X: the Lateran acts give it with long s read as f and a garbled Greek column, so every Latin quote carries the OCR noise.

A primary source for the letter in which Heraclius says the Ecthesis was not his (Baronius or Pagi's own text, or the letter itself): the Library has it only as a Latin quotation inside Mansi's notes.
A source for Bonaventure's birth year and for his own dates that is not a later chronicle (the Library headers say c. 1217-1274 but no text line gives a birth year).
flags: LINKS NOT CHANGED, already set: alexandria-catechetical--palestinian-church-pre-constantinian has concerns 'origen' and palestinian-church-pre-constantinian--hieronymian-ascetic-literary has concerns 'jerome'. Both notes name Pamphilus (his library and his copies of Origen), so each link also fits Pamphilus, but each stays with its present person. No concerns written for Pamphilus.

BONAVENTURE concerns: set on canons-regular-victorine-school--the-franciscan-movement (its note and sources are about his Itinerarium and McCann's remark on him). Not set on cistercian-monasticism--the-english-mystics-and-devout: two of its quoted sources name St. Bonaventura (Underhill, Rolle 1914 and Hilton 1923) but its note and main subject are Bernard, and Bernard has no entry; left null for the coordinator to decide. The entry's legacy uses those two Underhill lines.

HERACLIUS concerns: none set. byzantine-imperial-church-justinianic--byzantine-imperial-church-heraclian-iconoclast names him only to date the patriarchate's run (Sergius crowned him in 610); its quotes are the 681 council on Sergius and Macler's coronation note, so it is about Sergius and the patriarchate, not his own words or acts.

PEOPLE ROWS: alexandria-catechetical and byzantine-imperial-church-heraclian-iconoclast have no item for these two, so the items are added (replace_name null). Suggested order: Pamphilus after Dionysius of Alexandria (year about 307) and before Athanasius; Heraclius before Maximus the Confessor (year 610). Bonaventure replaces the existing row item named 'Bonaventure' (the McCann note citation).

LATIN, FRENCH AND ITALIAN: no English rendering of my own is quoted. Where the prose states what a Latin, French or Italian line says (Glassberger on his election, death and the 1269 chapter; the Itinerarium prologue; the Ecthesis and the Lateran council's words; Sebeos on the Cross; Serpos; the Chronicle of Seert), it is a plain statement of the line in the fact table, and each such row is marked 'plain gloss'. A Latin reader should check those rows before release.

PAMPHILUS dates: 307-310 are the prison years and the two dates given for his death (309 by Jerome's note and the anf06 notice; February 310 by the English editor of Eusebius, NPNF, from Martyrs of Palestine 11). start 307, end 310. The Library's sources give no birth year, so these are working years, not life years. The Lommatzsch file header also dates him d. 310.

PAMPHILUS lane: kept at the home tradition's lane (4 Africa), as origen does, though his life was at Caesarea (the Palestinian pre-Constantinian entry sits in lane 3). regions are Middle East and Mediterranean; modernCountries is Caesarea Maritima, copied from origen.

PAMPHILUS authorship (Mark's ruling B): the entry says plainly that the Library counts the jointly written Apology as his own words and names Jerome's denial. It also records that Jerome's own catalogue entry (De viris illustribus 75) gives Pamphilus an Apology for Origen, and that the English editors of Eusebius (McGiffert) and of Jerome and Rufinus (Freemantle) both hold that Pamphilus was a joint author. Jerome's catalogue line has italics tags inside the XML, so its fact row quotes the plain text before the tag. The passage about him copying Origen is Jerome too (De viris illustribus 75).

PAMPHILUS: the Apology's preface is headed 'Praefatio ad Confessores ad metalla Palaestinae damnatos' (Lommatzsch line 14112; Migne line 41939). I left it out of the prose because stating it needs my own English rendering of a Latin heading. It could be added if Mark accepts a plain gloss.

HERACLIUS dates: the brief said 610-641 was unsourced. Both ends are now tied to Library lines: coronation on 6 October 610 (Macler's note, Sebeos file line 4565) and death on 11 February 641 (a Latin note in Mansi X, line 73454-73455, OCR 'xt.' for 'xi.'). The earlier doubt about the Chronicle of Seert's printed year 992 of Alexander is settled by Scher's own footnote on the same page, which reads (OCR) 'plutot 952; Heraclius mourut le 11 fevrier'; 952 of Alexander is 640-41, so the Seert passage agrees with 641.

HERACLIUS legacy: Serpos line 16119-16120 and lines 13733-13738 are Italian OCR. The Chronicle of Seert passages are French OCR with garbled letters (for example 'tautiuople'); the quotes are verbatim to that OCR. Scher's death passage also appears in the Library's file with OCR damage.

NO NEW LINKS: none of the three entries' prose states a relationship between two traditions that the census lacks. The Armenian and Church of the East 'names him' relations are legacy statements only, not links.

BONAVENTURE legacy and sourcing: Liguori's sentence names no work (checked in the sentence at line 511); I did not check what Liguori cites elsewhere. The Underhill lines are from the introductions in the 1914 Rolle (Comper) and 1923 Hilton volumes, as the existing link note says.

HERACLIUS Ecthesis: Mansi X (line 63221 and lines 71322-71325) says a synod of Sergius in 638 confirmed the Ecthesis; the entry dates the confirmation, not the issue. The Ecthesis text in the Lateran acts begins about line 100116. The 'one operation or two' and 'two wills' sentences are the document's own words (Latin, OCR).

HERACLIUS authorship: the entry gives both sides (Lateran fathers: Sergius persuaded Heraclius to put his name to it; a letter quoted in Mansi's notes, in which Heraclius says he did not dictate it or order it made, that Sergius composed it, and that he agreed to set it out in his name with his signature). It counts as issued in his name under answer C.

BONAVENTURE dates: 1257 is Glassberger's 1256 corrected by the Quaracchi editors' note and Salimbene's 'seventeen years'. 1274 as the end year follows the Glassberger text of his death at the council; the editors' note puts the cardinalate in 1273 and the arrival at Lyon in November 1273.
